title: Frequency-Selective Woven Bamboo and Palm-Leaf Partitions for Sensory-Supportive Post-Disaster Shelters: Participatory Acoustic Co-Design for Neurodivergent Children in Rural Lombok
content: Neurodivergent children housed in post-disaster emergency shelters experience heightened sensory dysregulation driven by abrupt, high-frequency transient noises, yet standard open-plan tent interiors provide virtually no acoustic protection. This study introduces acoustically tuned woven bamboo and palm-leaf partitions designed to operate simultaneously as visual zoning dividers and frequency-selective acoustic filters—attenuating unpredictable transient noise across the 2–8 kHz band while retaining predictable low-frequency ambient sound between 50 and 250 Hz. Parameterized by weave porosity, fibre diameter, panel thickness, and channel tortuosity, each partition's acoustic behavior is predicted using an equivalent-fluid formulation whose flow resistivity follows a Kozeny–Carman-type relation. A perceptually weighted transmission target derived from children's measured sensory profiles guides parameter optimization under structural integrity and rapid-deployment mass constraints. Local weaving artisans co-fabricate prototypes across a factorial design grid and iteratively adjust weave density and strip dimensions using portable impedance- tube measurements, closing a human-in-the-loop optimization cycle. Full-scale mock shelter trials with neurodivergent children evaluate autonomic sensory regulation via high-frequency heart rate variability (HRV) and salivary cortisol, correlating physiological outcomes directly against measured transmission-loss spectra. Explicit substitution pathways integrate these partitions into conventional shelters: timber frame spacing defines geometric boundary conditions, ventilation and lighting systems supply the baseline soundscape, and the resulting transmission profile informs interior zoning and signage. Together, these findings establish an evidence-based methodology uniting acoustic material engineering, local craft knowledge, and community-based participatory design to deliver tunable sensory interventions for vulnerable children in rural Lombok.
